sections.title: Headline
sections.content: A single verified paper reports two antibody lead-optimization campaigns in which a general-purpose AI agent and a research team brought scientific reasoning into the lab-in-the-loop, uncovering that one thermal metric per scaffold did not measure what its name implied.

sections.title: Reasoning in the loop: antibody lead optimization by probing mechanism and measurement
sections.problem: Lab-in-the-loop antibody optimization depends on instrument-derived metrics as proxies for drug-relevant properties; when a metric is a poor proxy, better models or more data cannot fix it, and detecting the problem typically requires expert review.
sections.method: Two campaigns on BigHat Biosciences' Milliner platform (anti-albumin VHH and anti-mesothelin scFv) in which a research team and a general-purpose AI agent, Claude, brought scientific reasoning into the loop; libraries were built from antibody lineage, structure and biophysics as controlled comparisons, a physical model of the raw assay curves was fit to select scaffold-suited metrics, and the experimental protocol was changed (protein concentration, heating rate) to test the model against pre-registered predictions.
sections.key_result: Over seven rounds and about 1,010 design variants, raw curves revealed that on each scaffold one thermal metric did not measure what its name implied; the controlled comparisons also show what each mutation contributes to each property, and both leads improve on their parents in affinity, thermal stability and aggregation while improving or maintaining yield and purity.
sections.caveat: Results are reported by the authors for two campaigns on one company's platform and have not been independently replicated here; the abstract does not quantify the improvements, and the AI agent's specific contribution relative to the research team is not isolated in the supplied metadata.
sections.why_it_matters: It frames metric validity, not model capacity, as the binding constraint in lab-in-the-loop optimization and demonstrates a workflow for diagnosing proxy failure with mechanistic reasoning and pre-registered tests.

sections.title: Takeaway
sections.content: The week's only qualifying paper argues that in lab-in-the-loop antibody optimization the decisive failure mode is a metric that misrepresents the property it names, which neither better models nor more data can repair. Its response is to fold scientific reasoning, including an AI agent, into the loop, fit a physical model of the raw curves, and validate revised metrics and protocols against pre-registered predictions. The reported gains are author-reported from two campaigns on a single platform and are not quantified in the supplied metadata.
